etymology: Coined by the evolutionary biologist Richard Dawkins in The Selfish Gene (1976), from Greek mimēma (a thing imitated), shortened to rhyme with gene: a unit of culture, an idea or habit that spreads by imitation as genes spread by reproduction. Mike Godwin applied it to the internet in a 1994 Wired article. In the 2000s meme came to mean a shareable joke format, usually an image with a caption (the "image macro"), endlessly copied and remixed; by the 2010s memes were the Millennial lingua franca and, increasingly, a tool of politics and advertising.
biblical_def: A meme is a joke, image, or phrase that spreads by being copied and remixed: the captioned cat, the distracted-boyfriend photo, the format everyone fills with their own punchline. For Millennials memes became a language, a way to say in one picture what would take a paragraph. The Christian observation has two parts. First, the word carries a worldview. Dawkins coined it to explain human culture, including religion, as replicating units competing for survival, with no Mind behind them; he called faith a mind-virus. Christians reject that account: ideas are not mindless replicators but the thoughts of image-bearers who are responsible for them. "For as he thinketh in his heart, so is he" (Pro 23:7). Second, the internet meme itself is morally neutral and powerful. A good meme can be genuinely funny and even wise; Proverbs is a collection of compact, memorable sayings that spread from mouth to mouth. But memes also spread mockery, falsehood, and cynicism at a speed no proverb ever did, and they shape thinking below the level of argument. "Every idle word that men shall speak, they shall give account thereof" (Mat 12:36), and that includes every idle image shared. Paul’s rule for the mind applies to the feed: "whatsoever things are true … whatsoever things are lovely … think on these things" (Php 4:8). A father laughs at a good meme with his son and asks him, now and then, "Is that true? Is it kind? Would you say it to the person’s face?" He teaches him to notice what the memes he consumes are teaching him to believe.
webster_summary: Dawkins’s 1976 coinage (Greek mimēma) for a self-replicating unit of culture, turned Millennial internet word for a shareable joke format; the internet meme is neutral and powerful, but Dawkins’s mindless-replicator account of ideas is false, and every shared word is accountable (Mat 12:36).
webster_full: MEME, n. (coined 1976; Millennial internet sense, 2000s–present) (1) An idea or behaviour that spreads by imitation (Dawkins). (2) A humorous image, video, or text format copied and varied online. Also to meme, memeable, dank memes.

Webster (1828), root mimic: MIMIC, noun One who imitates or mimics; a buffoon who attempts to excite laughter or derision by acting or speaking in the manner of another. 1. A mean or servile imitator. Of France the mimic and of Spain the prey.
Decode for parents: memes teach beliefs without arguments; ask your children what the ones they share are saying.
scriptures: For as he thinketh in his heart, so is he: Eat and drink, saith he to thee; but his heart is not with thee.
But I say unto you, That every idle word that men shall speak, they shall give account thereof in the day of judgment.

Finally, brethren, whatsoever things are true, whatsoever things are honest, whatsoever things are just, whatsoever things are pure, whatsoever things are lovely, whatsoever things are of good report; if there be any virtue, and if there be any praise, think on these things.
To understand a proverb, and the interpretation; the words of the wise, and their dark sayings.
Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men, after the rudiments of the world, and not after Christ.
corruption_summary: Meme carries Dawkins’s account of ideas as mindless replicators, and its internet form spreads mockery and falsehood below the level of argument; Scripture makes every thought and shared word accountable.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is double. At the root is a philosophy: Dawkins designed the word to explain belief, especially faith, as a kind of contagion that survives because it spreads, not because it is true. Paul warned of exactly such frameworks: "Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men" (Col 2:8). At the surface is a habit: memes persuade by laughter and repetition rather than by reasons, so a generation can absorb a whole set of attitudes, toward faith, marriage, authority, and the opposite sex, without ever hearing an argument.

The redemption is wisdom in compact form. Proverbs exists "To understand a proverb, and the interpretation; the words of the wise, and their dark sayings" (Pro 1:6): God Himself uses memorable, shareable sayings. Christians can make and enjoy good memes, funny, true, and kind ones, and they can teach their children to read memes critically, asking what each one assumes and whether it is true. The antidote to a bad meme is often a better proverb.
roots_summary: Greek mimēma (thing imitated) → Dawkins’s meme (1976, rhyming with gene) → Godwin, Wired (1994) → 2000s image macros → 2010s Millennial lingua franca.
roots_lines: Greek mimeisthai — to imitate; mimēma — that which is imitated
1976: Richard Dawkins, The Selfish Gene, coins meme
1994: Mike Godwin applies it to internet culture
2000s–2010s: image macros, reaction images, formats; memes as politics and advertising
Biblical anchor: as he thinketh in his heart, so is he (Pro 23:7); every idle word (Mat 12:36)
usage: "Did you see the meme about Mondays?"
Proverbs are God’s memes: compact, true, and meant to spread (Pro 1:6).
Beware philosophy after the tradition of men (Col 2:8), even when it is funny.

etymology: A bait-and-switch prank: a link promising one thing leads instead to the music video for Rick Astley’s 1987 hit "Never Gonna Give You Up." It grew out of a 2006–2007 4chan prank called the duckroll and took its own form in May 2007. YouTube rickrolled every featured video on April Fools’ Day 2008; Astley himself rickrolled the 2008 Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade. The video has since passed a billion views, and the prank remains the classic Millennial internet joke.
biblical_def: To rickroll someone is to trick him into clicking a link that turns out to be Rick Astley singing "Never Gonna Give You Up." The victim groans; the prankster laughs; nobody is hurt. It is the most innocent of the internet’s practical jokes, and it has lasted for nearly two decades. The Christian observation: harmless pranks between friends are part of ordinary human fun, and Scripture does not forbid laughter at a well-turned surprise. The only principle to keep in view is the one Proverbs states about deception that is not harmless: "As a mad man who casteth firebrands, arrows, and death, So is the man that deceiveth his neighbour, and saith, Am not I in sport?" (Pro 26:18-19). A rickroll is the opposite of a firebrand, which is why it is beloved. But the same bait-and-switch technique is used by scammers, phishing links, and clickbait, and teaching children to recognize a rickroll is not a bad first lesson in internet discernment. There is also an accidental sermon in the song. The prank promises "never gonna give you up, never gonna let you down," lines no human lover can guarantee. God made that promise and keeps it: "I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee" (Heb 13:5); "For the mountains shall depart, and the hills be removed; but my kindness shall not depart from thee" (Isa 54:10). A father can enjoy rickrolling his kids and, once in a while, point out that the only One who will never give them up is the Lord.
webster_summary: Millennial internet prank (2007; YouTube April Fools 2008) luring someone to Rick Astley’s "Never Gonna Give You Up"; harmless fun, a first lesson in spotting bait-and-switch, and an accidental echo of God’s promise never to forsake (Heb 13:5).
webster_full: RICKROLL, v.t. / n. (Millennial internet slang, 2007–present) To trick someone into opening a link to the music video for Rick Astley’s "Never Gonna Give You Up" (1987); the prank itself. Precursor: duckroll (4chan, 2006).

Webster (1828), root roll: ROLL, verb transitive [It is usual to consider this word as formed by contraction from the Latin rotula, a little wheel, from rota.] 1. To move by turning on the surface, or with a circular motion in which all parts of the surface are successively applied to a plane; as, to roll a barrel or puncheon; to roll a stone or ball. Sisyphus was condemned to roll a stone to the top of a hill, which, when he had done so, rolled down again, and thus his punishment was eternal. 2. To revolve; to turn on its axis; […]
Decode for parents: harmless fun, and a chance to teach children to recognize bait-and-switch links that are not harmless.
scriptures: As a mad man who casteth firebrands, arrows, and death, So is the man that deceiveth his neighbour, and saith, Am not I in sport?
Let your conversation be without covetousness; and be content with such things as ye have: for he hath said, I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee.
For the mountains shall depart, and the hills be removed; but my kindness shall not depart from thee, neither shall the covenant of my peace be removed, saith the LORD that hath mercy on thee.
A merry heart doeth good like a medicine: but a broken spirit drieth the bones.
Behold, I send you forth as sheep in the midst of wolves: be ye therefore wise as serpents, and harmless as doves.
corruption_summary: The rickroll is a harmless prank; its technique, the bait-and-switch, is the same one scams use, and its song accidentally echoes a promise only God keeps.
corruption_paragraphs: There is little to correct in the rickroll itself; it is a joke in which everyone is in on the joke within seconds. The shadow lies in the technique. Clickbait, phishing, and scams all work the same way: a promise that turns out to be something else. Children who learn to laugh at the harmless version should also learn to spot the dangerous one. "Behold, I send you forth as sheep in the midst of wolves: be ye therefore wise as serpents, and harmless as doves" (Mat 10:16).

The redemption is an unexpected one. A billion people have heard a pop song promise never to give them up, never to let them down, never to run around and desert them. No human singer can keep that promise. God can, and does. Let the joke become a doorway: the faithful love the song only sings about is real, and it is found in Christ, who will never leave nor forsake His own.
roots_summary: Rick (Astley) + roll (from 4chan’s duckroll) → rickroll (May 2007) → YouTube April Fools 2008 → enduring internet prank.
roots_lines: Latin rotula (little wheel) → roll; 4chan duckroll (2006) bait-and-switch
1987: Rick Astley, "Never Gonna Give You Up"
May 2007: rickroll emerges; 2008: YouTube April Fools; Macy’s parade
2020s: the video passes a billion views; prank still current
Biblical anchor: I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee (Heb 13:5)
usage: "I clicked his ‘test answers’ link and got rickrolled."
The song promises never to give you up; only God keeps that promise (Heb 13:5).
Wise as serpents, harmless as doves (Mat 10:16): learn to spot the bait.

etymology: A photograph of a cat with a caption in deliberately broken English ("lolspeak"), from LOL + cat. It grew out of 4chan’s "Caturday" image threads around 2005–2006; the site I Can Has Cheezburger?, launched in January 2007 and named for its most famous caption, made lolcats a mass phenomenon and an internet business. Lolspeak spread widely ("I can has," "ceiling cat is watching you," "invisible bike"). A crowd-sourced LOLCat Bible Translation Project (begun 2007) rendered Scripture in lolspeak.
biblical_def: A lolcat is a cat photo with a misspelled, baby-talk caption: "I can has cheezburger?" The genre was the Millennial internet’s first great comic form, and it turned house cats into an industry. The Christian observation: much of this is innocent and even good. Delight in animals is a biblical thing. God made the creatures and saw that they were good; He gave man dominion over them with responsibility, and "A righteous man regardeth the life of his beast" (Pro 12:10). The Lord feeds the birds and knows the sparrow’s fall (Mat 10:29). Laughing at a cat’s absurdities is a small enjoyment of creation. Two cautions are worth noting. The first is time: lolcats were the beginning of the endless scroll of cute and funny animals, and an evening of it is an evening gone. "Redeeming the time, because the days are evil" (Eph 5:16). The second is irreverence: lolspeak culture produced a running joke in which God was "Ceiling Cat," and a full lolspeak paraphrase of the Bible. Christians can laugh at cats and still refuse to make the Lord a punchline. "Holy and reverend is his name" (Psa 111:9). A father lets his children enjoy the funny cat pictures, teaches them to care for real animals kindly, and makes sure they know that the Creator of the cat is not a joke.
webster_summary: Millennial internet genre (4chan c. 2005; I Can Has Cheezburger?, 2007) of captioned cat photos in "lolspeak"; innocent delight in creation (Pro 12:10), with cautions about wasted time and lolspeak’s irreverent "Ceiling Cat" jokes about God (Psa 111:9).
webster_full: LOLCAT, n. (Millennial internet slang, c. 2005–2010s) A photograph of a cat with a humorous caption in deliberately ungrammatical English. Related: lolspeak, "I can has cheezburger?", Caturday.

Webster (1828), root cat: CAT, noun 1. A name applied to certain species of carnivorous quadrupeds, of the genus Felis. The domestic cat needs no description. It is a deceitful animal, and when enraged, extremely spiteful. It is kept in houses, chiefly for the purpose of catching rats and mice. The wild cat is much larger than the domestic cat It is a strong, ferocious animal, living in the forest, and very destructive to poultry and lambs. The wild cat of Europe is of the same species with the domestic cat; […]
Decode for parents: enjoy the cats; keep God out of the punchline.
scriptures: A righteous man regardeth the life of his beast: but the tender mercies of the wicked are cruel.
And God made the beast of the earth after his kind, and cattle after their kind, and every thing that creepeth upon the earth after his kind: and God saw that it was good.
Are not two sparrows sold for a farthing? and one of them shall not fall on the ground without your Father.
Redeeming the time, because the days are evil.
He sent redemption unto his people: he hath commanded his covenant for ever: holy and reverend is his name.
corruption_summary: Lolcats are innocent delight in God’s creatures; their shadows are hours lost to the scroll and a lolspeak culture that made God a joke.
corruption_paragraphs: The small corruptions are time and reverence. The captioned cat began a stream of cute content that never ends, and an endless stream is a thief of hours. The lolspeak culture around it also made a habit of turning God into a joke character, and a generation that laughed at "Ceiling Cat" was learning, a little, to treat the Lord as material. That is not a small thing to the One who said He would not hold guiltless those who take His name in vain.

The redemption is wonder at the creatures. "And God made the beast of the earth after his kind, and cattle after their kind, and every thing that creepeth upon the earth after his kind: and God saw that it was good" (Gen 1:25). Cats are funny because God made them so. Teach children to laugh at the cat, to feed and care for it well, to put down the phone when the scroll has gone on too long, and to give thanks to the Maker of every whisker.
roots_summary: LOL + cat (Old English catt) → 4chan "Caturday" (c. 2005) → I Can Has Cheezburger? (2007) → lolspeak culture.
roots_lines: Old English catt, Late Latin cattus — the domestic cat
c. 2005–2006: 4chan "Caturday" captioned cat threads
January 2007: I Can Has Cheezburger? launches
2007–: lolspeak; the LOLCat Bible Translation Project
Biblical anchor: a righteous man regardeth the life of his beast (Pro 12:10)
usage: "Remember lolcats? ‘I can has cheezburger?’"
God saw that it was good (Gen 1:25), cats included.
Holy and reverend is his name (Psa 111:9): not "Ceiling Cat."

etymology: An internet misspelling of dog (used in a 2005 Homestar Runner episode) attached in 2013 to a 2010 photograph of Kabosu, a Shiba Inu belonging to the Japanese kindergarten teacher Atsuko Sato. The meme set the dog’s sideways glance among multicoloured Comic Sans phrases in broken English: "such wow," "much amaze," "very fun." In December 2013 two programmers created Dogecoin as a joke cryptocurrency; it later became an object of real speculation. Kabosu died in May 2024. The English word doge also names the elected chief magistrate of Venice.
biblical_def: Doge is the Shiba Inu meme: a dog looking sideways, surrounded by Comic Sans fragments like "such wow" and "much amaze." It was the internet’s favourite joke of 2013 and spawned a joke cryptocurrency, Dogecoin, which later made and lost fortunes. The Christian observation: the meme itself is gentle nonsense, a dog and some broken grammar, and there is nothing wrong with enjoying it. It also offers three small lessons. First, the dog. Kabosu was a real animal, loved by her owner, and the whole internet delighted in her face. The Lord made the creatures for His glory and our good, and "A righteous man regardeth the life of his beast" (Pro 12:10). Second, the coin. A joke became a market, and many young men poured savings into it hoping to get rich quickly. Scripture warns plainly: "Wealth gotten by vanity shall be diminished: but he that gathereth by labour shall increase" (Pro 13:11); "he that maketh haste to be rich shall not be innocent" (Pro 28:20). Third, the word. In Webster’s 1828 dictionary, doge was "The chief magistrate of Venice and Genoa," a ruler. It is a small parable of how quickly the grand becomes the silly, and how the powers of this world pass away while the Lord reigns. A father enjoys the meme with his children, teaches them to treat animals kindly, and warns his sons that a joke coin is not an investment strategy.
webster_summary: Millennial meme (2013) of the Shiba Inu Kabosu with Comic Sans "such wow" captions, which spawned Dogecoin; gentle nonsense, with a real warning against haste to be rich (Pro 28:20) and a reminder that Webster’s doge was a Venetian ruler.
webster_full: DOGE, n. (Millennial internet slang, 2013–present; misspelling of dog) The meme of a Shiba Inu with captions in broken English and Comic Sans ("such wow, much amaze"). Related: Dogecoin (2013).
Webster (1828), root doge: DOGE, noun [Latin , to lead.] The chief magistrate of Venice and Genoa.
Decode for parents: enjoy the dog; warn your sons about joke coins and get-rich-quick schemes.
scriptures: A righteous man regardeth the life of his beast: but the tender mercies of the wicked are cruel.
Wealth gotten by vanity shall be diminished: but he that gathereth by labour shall increase.
A faithful man shall abound with blessings: but he that maketh haste to be rich shall not be innocent.
Put not your trust in princes, nor in the son of man, in whom there is no help. His breath goeth forth, he returneth to his earth; in that very day his thoughts perish.
He that loveth silver shall not be satisfied with silver; nor he that loveth abundance with increase: this is also vanity.
corruption_summary: Doge is gentle nonsense; its offspring, a joke cryptocurrency, became a speculative mania, against Scripture’s warnings on haste to be rich.
corruption_paragraphs: The meme has no real vice; its one corruption came through the coin. Dogecoin began as satire and became a casino, driven by celebrity posts and online crowds, and many young men learned that wealth comes from catching a wave rather than from work. Scripture’s verdict on that hope is steady: "He that loveth silver shall not be satisfied with silver; nor he that loveth abundance with increase: this is also vanity" (Ecc 5:10).

The redemption is to laugh and to learn. Laugh at the dog, and remember that God made her. Learn from the coin that quick money is usually quick loss, and that steady labour and generous giving are the biblical path. And learn from the old word that rulers and their titles pass: "Put not your trust in princes … His breath goeth forth, he returneth to his earth" (Psa 146:3-4). The doge of Venice is a meme now; the Lord reigns for ever.
roots_summary: Latin dux (leader) → Venetian doge (chief magistrate) / separately, dog misspelled doge (2005) → 2013 Shiba Inu meme → Dogecoin.
roots_lines: Latin dux — leader → Venetian doge — the elected ruler of Venice
2005: doge as a jokey misspelling of dog (Homestar Runner)
2010 photo of Kabosu; 2013: the doge meme, "such wow, much amaze"
December 2013: Dogecoin; 2020s: speculative surges; May 2024: Kabosu dies
Biblical anchor: he that maketh haste to be rich shall not be innocent (Pro 28:20)
usage: "Such wow. Very meme. Much doge."
Wealth gotten by vanity shall be diminished (Pro 13:11).
Put not your trust in princes (Psa 146:3), or in doges.

etymology: A photo fad in which a person lies face down, rigid as a board, arms at the sides, in an unusual or public place, and is photographed. Versions called the "lying down game" circulated in Britain in the 2000s; the name planking and the global craze came from Australia in 2011, spreading through Facebook. It peaked that summer and faded quickly. In May 2011 a young man in Brisbane died after falling from a seventh-floor balcony railing while attempting a plank, drawing worldwide attention to the fad’s dangers. (The fitness exercise called a "plank" is a separate usage.)
biblical_def: Planking was the 2011 fad of lying stiff and face down in odd places, on a railing, a car roof, a fast-food counter, and posting the photo. It was mostly silly and harmless, the kind of joke that is funny for a summer. The Christian observation: the fad is a small case study in two things Scripture cares about. The first is the pull of the crowd toward foolishness. Most planking was harmless, but the escalation was predictable: higher railings, busier roads, more dangerous ledges, because the photo had to top the last one. A young man died. The sixth commandment, "Thou shalt not kill" (Exo 20:13), forbids not only murder but, as the Reformed catechisms teach, the reckless endangering of one’s own life and the lives of others. The Westminster Larger Catechism lists among its duties "all careful studies, and lawful endeavours, to preserve the life of ourselves and others." The Lord Jesus refused to throw Himself from the temple’s pinnacle to prove something: "It is written again, Thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God" (Mat 4:7). The second is the strange power of the camera to make ordinary people do absurd and risky things for an audience. "The prudent man looketh well to his going" (Pro 14:15). A father lets his children laugh at a harmless fad and teaches them where the line is: no picture is worth a life, and no audience is worth risking the body God gave you.
webster_summary: Millennial photo fad (Australia, 2011) of lying rigid in odd places; mostly silly, but its deadly escalation illustrates the sixth commandment’s duty to preserve life (Exo 20:13) and Christ’s refusal to tempt God for a spectacle (Mat 4:7).
webster_full: PLANKING, n. (Millennial internet fad, 2011) Lying face down and rigid in an unusual or public place to be photographed. Precursor: the "lying down game" (UK, 2000s). Related stunts: owling, Tebowing.

Webster (1828), root plank: PLANK, noun A broad piece of sawed timber, differing from a board only in being thicker. In America, broad pieces of sawed timber which are not more than an inch or an inch and a quarter thick, are called boards; like pieces from an inch and a half to three or four inches thick, are called planks. Sometimes pieces more than four inches thick are called planks.
Decode for parents: talk about the line between a funny photo and a dangerous stunt before the next fad arrives.
scriptures: Jesus said unto him, It is written again, Thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God.
The simple believeth every word: but the prudent man looketh well to his going.
A prudent man foreseeth the evil, and hideth himself: but the simple pass on, and are punished.
What? know ye not that your body is the temple of the Holy Ghost which is in you, which ye have of God, and ye are not your own?
corruption_summary: Planking was a harmless joke that escalated into deadly stunts for the camera; Scripture’s duty to preserve life and Christ’s refusal to tempt God draw the line.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is escalation for an audience. Fads that reward novelty push participants to outdo each other, and the cheapest way to outdo is danger. The camera creates a crowd that is never present to say "stop." The planking deaths and injuries were not flukes but the logic of the fad worked out. Proverbs saw it long ago: "A prudent man foreseeth the evil, and hideth himself; but the simple pass on, and are punished" (Pro 22:3).

The redemption is prudence and stewardship. The body is the temple of the Holy Ghost (1Co 6:19), not a prop. Teach the young that it is fine to be silly, that daring has its place in good causes, and that risking life for a photo is a sin against the sixth commandment. When the next fad arrives, as it will, they should already have asked themselves the question: would I do this if no one were watching?
roots_summary: Late Latin planca (board) → plank → 2011 Australian planking craze (from the UK "lying down game") → fade after fatal accidents.
roots_lines: Late Latin planca — a board, a slab
2000s: UK "lying down game"
2011: planking craze from Australia via Facebook
May 2011: fatal fall in Brisbane; global attention to the dangers
Biblical anchor: thou shalt not kill (Exo 20:13); thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God (Mat 4:7)
usage: "They were planking on the picnic tables all summer."
Thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God (Mat 4:7): no photo is worth a life.
The prudent man looketh well to his going (Pro 14:15).

etymology: A 2014 viral campaign in which participants filmed themselves dumping a bucket of ice water over their heads, nominated others to do the same within twenty-four hours, and donated to amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) research. It was popularized in July–August 2014 by Pete Frates, a former Boston College baseball captain with ALS, and Pat Quinn of New York, who also had the disease. More than seventeen million videos were posted and the ALS Association received about $115 million. Some Christian leaders cautioned that the Association funded embryonic stem-cell research and directed gifts to other ALS charities.
biblical_def: The Ice Bucket Challenge was the great viral charity event of 2014: film yourself getting soaked with ice water, nominate three friends, and donate to fight ALS. Celebrities, athletes, politicians, and millions of ordinary people joined. The Christian observation has more than one side. On the good side, real money went to research for a cruel disease, and men who were dying, Pete Frates and Pat Quinn, saw their friends rally around them. Scripture commends generosity: "He which soweth bountifully shall reap also bountifully … for God loveth a cheerful giver" (2Co 9:6-7). On the side that deserves examination: first, the challenge mixed giving with self-display, filmed and posted, when the Lord Jesus said, "when thou doest alms, let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doeth: That thine alms may be in secret" (Mat 6:3-4). Many took the challenge and never gave at all. Second, the ethics of where the money went mattered. Some Christians noted that the beneficiary funded research on human embryos, and directed their gifts to ALS charities that respect the life of the unborn. That was not killjoy; it was obedience to the sixth commandment and to the truth that God forms life in the womb (Psa 139:13). A father teaches his children to give generously, to give mostly in secret, and to ask where their gifts go, so that compassion for one suffering person is never paid for with the lives of the smallest.
webster_summary: Millennial viral charity campaign (summer 2014) for ALS: ice water, nominations, donations; real generosity (2Co 9:7) mixed with public display (Mat 6:3-4), with a Christian caution about embryonic research funding (Psa 139:13).
webster_full: ICE BUCKET CHALLENGE, n. (Millennial viral campaign, 2014) A filmed challenge to pour ice water over one’s head, nominate others, and donate to ALS research. Raised about $115 million for the ALS Association.

Webster (1828), root challenge: CHALLENGE, noun Literally, a calling, or crying out, the primary sense of many words expressing a demand, as claim. Hence appropriately, 1. A calling upon one to fight in single combat; an invitation or summons, verbal or written, to decide a controversy by a duel. Hence the letter containing the summons is also called a challenge 2. A claim or demand made of a right or supposed right. There must be no challenge of superiority. 3. Among hunters, the opening and crying of hounds at the first finding the scent of their game. […]
Decode for parents: teach your children to give generously, quietly, and wisely, asking where their gifts go.
scriptures: Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.
But when thou doest alms, let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doeth: That thine alms may be in secret: and thy Father which seeth in secret himself shall reward thee openly.
For thou hast possessed my reins: thou hast covered me in my mother's womb.
As we have therefore opportunity, let us do good unto all men, especially unto them who are of the household of faith.
Withhold not good from them to whom it is due, when it is in the power of thine hand to do it.
corruption_summary: The Ice Bucket Challenge joined real generosity to public display and, for some, to morally troubling research; Scripture asks for cheerful, secret, and conscientious giving.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the merger of charity and performance. The challenge’s genius was that it made giving shareable; its weakness was that sharing could replace giving. The video became the point, the donation optional. A culture of "awareness" can feel virtuous while doing little. And generosity without discernment can fund wrong things: compassion for the sick must never be purchased with the destruction of human embryos, who are lives formed by God.

The redemption is generous, wise, and humble giving. "Withhold not good from them to whom it is due, when it is in the power of thine hand to do it" (Pro 3:27). Christians should be the first to help the sick, including those with ALS, and the most careful about how. Teach the young to give from their own money, to do much of it in secret, to research charities, and to love the suffering neighbour in ways that honour every human life.
roots_summary: Old French chalenge (accusation, claim) → challenge (a call to contest) → 2014 Ice Bucket Challenge (Frates, Quinn) → viral-charity template.
roots_lines: Latin calumnia → Old French chalenge — a claim, a summons
2014: Pete Frates and Pat Quinn popularize the ALS challenge
July–August 2014: 17 million videos; about $115 million raised
Christian caution: embryonic stem-cell funding; redirected gifts
Biblical anchor: God loveth a cheerful giver (2Co 9:7); let not thy left hand know (Mat 6:3)
usage: "Remember when everyone did the Ice Bucket Challenge?"
Let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doeth (Mat 6:3).
Thou hast covered me in my mother’s womb (Psa 139:13): give to help the sick without harming the smallest.

etymology: A dance move in which a person drops the head into the crook of one bent elbow while extending the other arm upward and outward, like a sneeze. It came from the Atlanta hip-hop scene about 2014 (credited variously to Skippa Da Flippa and to Migos, whose "Look at My Dab" appeared in 2015). Carolina Panthers quarterback Cam Newton’s touchdown dabs in the 2015 NFL season made it a national craze, and by 2016 politicians, grandparents, and schoolchildren were dabbing for the camera. It faded by 2017 as an ironic Millennial gesture. (Unrelated: dab as slang for a cannabis concentrate.)
biblical_def: To dab is to strike the pose: head ducked into one elbow, other arm flung out. In 2015–2016 it was everywhere: in end zones, classrooms, graduation photos, and campaign events. The Christian observation: a dance move is not a moral question, and the dab was a harmless, silly celebration. Scripture is not against celebration or dancing; Miriam took a timbrel and the women "went out after her with timbrels and with dances" (Exo 15:20), and David danced before the LORD. Two small notes are worth making. First, celebration in Scripture is aimed somewhere, at a victory given by God. The dab as a touchdown gesture often celebrated the self, and sportsmanship includes humility in winning: "Let another man praise thee, and not thine own mouth" (Pro 27:2). Second, the same three letters carry a darker slang meaning among teenagers: a dab is a highly concentrated form of cannabis, inhaled through a special rig, and "dabbing" in that sense is dangerous. A parent who hears the word should know which one is meant. Paul’s rule fits both: "whether therefore ye eat, or drink, or whatsoever ye do, do all to the glory of God" (1Co 10:31), and "Be sober, be vigilant" (1Pe 5:8). A father dabs badly at his son’s graduation to make him groan, and also knows enough to ask a careful question if he hears about "dabs" at a party.
webster_summary: Millennial dance move (Atlanta hip-hop c. 2014; Cam Newton, 2015) of ducking the head into an elbow; harmless celebration, best aimed at thanks rather than self (Pro 27:2); note the separate, dangerous cannabis sense of dab.
webster_full: DAB, n. / v.i. (Millennial slang, c. 2014–2017) A celebratory dance gesture: the head dropped into the crook of a bent arm, the other arm extended. "He dabbed in the end zone."
Separate slang sense: a concentrated cannabis extract; dabbing = inhaling it.
Webster (1828), root dab: DAB, verb transitive 1. To strike gently with the hand; to slap; to box. 2. To strike gently with some soft or moist substance; as, to dab a sore with lint.
Decode for parents: the dance is harmless; the drug sense is not; know which one you are hearing.
scriptures: And Miriam the prophetess, the sister of Aaron, took a timbrel in her hand; and all the women went out after her with timbrels and with dances.
Let another man praise thee, and not thine own mouth; a stranger, and not thine own lips.
Whether therefore ye eat, or drink, or whatsoever ye do, do all to the glory of God.
Be sober, be vigilant; because your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, walketh about, seeking whom he may devour:
Thou hast turned for me my mourning into dancing: thou hast put off my sackcloth, and girded me with gladness;
corruption_summary: The dab is a harmless dance; its only shadows are self-celebration and a same-spelled slang for concentrated cannabis that parents should recognize.
corruption_paragraphs: There is little to correct in the dance itself. The touchdown dab could become a taunt, a celebration of self at an opponent’s expense, and the gesture often said "look at me" more than "thank God." That is a small sin of pride, common to all sports celebrations. The more serious concern is the homonym: dabs of cannabis concentrate are far stronger than ordinary marijuana, and teenagers using the word may not mean the dance.

The redemption is joy with direction and sobriety with knowledge. "Thou hast turned for me my mourning into dancing: thou hast put off my sackcloth, and girded me with gladness" (Psa 30:11). Christians can dance, celebrate, and be silly; let the celebration remember the Giver. And parents should be vigilant, knowing the language of the culture well enough to recognize danger in it.
roots_summary: Middle English dabben (to strike gently) → dab → c. 2014 Atlanta hip-hop dance → 2015 Cam Newton → 2016 global craze.
roots_lines: Middle English dabben — to strike lightly, to pat
c. 2014: Atlanta hip-hop dance dab; 2015: Migos, "Look at My Dab"
2015 NFL season: Cam Newton’s touchdown dabs
2016: worldwide craze; 2017: fades to irony
Biblical anchor: thou hast turned for me my mourning into dancing (Psa 30:11)
usage: "The whole graduating class dabbed for the photo."
Let another man praise thee (Pro 27:2): even in the end zone.
Be sober, be vigilant (1Pe 5:8): know the other meaning of dab.

etymology: A trophy or medal given to every member of a team or every entrant in an event, regardless of performance. The practice grew in American youth sports from the 1980s and 1990s, when Millennials were children. By the 2010s participation trophy had become a byword for the supposed entitlement of the Millennial generation ("the participation-trophy generation"), and a political insult for anyone thought to expect reward without achievement. In 2015 the NFL linebacker James Harrison publicly returned his sons’ participation trophies.
biblical_def: A participation trophy is the medal every child gets for showing up; as an insult, it names a person who expects praise and reward without having earned them. Millennials were the first generation raised with them en masse, and they have heard the joke ever since. The Christian observation: the debate has more sides than either camp admits. Scripture does honour excellence and effort. "Know ye not that they which run in a race run all, but one receiveth the prize? So run, that ye may obtain" (1Co 9:24). Proverbs praises the diligent and warns that "The soul of the sluggard desireth, and hath nothing" (Pro 13:4). Children who are never allowed to lose are not prepared for life, and rewards that mean nothing teach that nothing means anything. Yet the gospel itself looks, at first glance, like a participation trophy: God gives eternal life not to the strong but to the undeserving, by grace. "For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast" (Eph 2:8-9). The difference is enormous. Grace is not a reward for showing up; it is a rescue for those who could not win, purchased by Christ, who did win. And grace produces effort: those saved by it are "created in Christ Jesus unto good works" (Eph 2:10), and they will hear "Well done, thou good and faithful servant" (Mat 25:21) for real faithfulness. A father lets his children lose, teaches them to work, celebrates their effort honestly, and tells them the good news that what they could never earn, Christ earned for them.
webster_summary: Millennial-era byword (1980s–90s youth sports; 2010s insult) for reward without achievement; Scripture prizes diligence and the race well run (1Co 9:24), and distinguishes grace, a rescue earned by Christ, from a trophy for showing up (Eph 2:8-10).
webster_full: PARTICIPATION TROPHY, n. (Millennial-era term, 1990s–present) A trophy given to every participant regardless of result; figuratively, praise or reward unearned. "The participation-trophy generation."

Webster (1828), root trophy: TROPHY, noun [Latin tropoeum.] 1. Among the ancients, a pile of arms taken from a vanquished enemy, raised on the field of battle by the conquerors; also, the representation of such a pile in marble, on medals and the like; or according to others, trophies were trees planted in conspicuous places of the conquered provinces, and hung with the spoils of the enemy, in memory of the victory. Hence, 2. Any thing taken and preserved as a memorial of victory, as arms, flags, standards and the like, taken from an enemy. […]
Decode for parents: let your children lose, praise real effort, and teach them grace is not a participation trophy.
scriptures: Know ye not that they which run in a race run all, but one receiveth the prize? So run, that ye may obtain.
The soul of the sluggard desireth, and hath nothing: but the soul of the diligent shall be made fat.
For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.
For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works, which God hath before ordained that we should walk in them.
His lord said unto him, Well done, thou good and faithful servant: thou hast been faithful over a few things, I will make thee ruler over many things: enter thou into the joy of thy lord.
corruption_summary: Participation trophies blur reward and effort and leave children unprepared for loss; the gospel’s grace is no trophy for showing up but a rescue that produces faithful work.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the separation of reward from reality. When every child gets the same medal, the medal stops meaning anything, and children learn that adults will pretend about results. Some grow up expecting affirmation without effort; others learn to despise the affirmation. Both lessons damage the soul’s understanding of work and reward, which Scripture treats as real: the sluggard desires and has nothing; the diligent are made fat.

The recovery is honesty and grace together. Let children compete, win, and lose, and teach them to lose well. Praise effort truthfully. And make sure they understand the gospel rightly: not that God hands out trophies to everyone who participates, but that Christ ran the race we could not finish and gives His victory to those who trust Him, who then run with all their strength out of gratitude. That is the opposite of entitlement.
roots_summary: Latin participare (to share in) + Greek tropaion (monument of a rout) → trophy → 1980s–90s youth-sports awards → 2010s generational insult.
roots_lines: Latin participatio — a sharing in
Greek tropaion — a monument set up where an enemy turned to flee → trophy
1980s–90s: participation awards spread in American youth sports
2010s: "participation-trophy generation"; 2015: James Harrison returns his sons’ trophies
Biblical anchor: so run, that ye may obtain (1Co 9:24); by grace are ye saved (Eph 2:8)
usage: "He expects a raise for showing up. Participation trophy."
So run, that ye may obtain (1Co 9:24).
Grace is not a trophy for participating; it is Christ’s victory given to the beaten (Eph 2:8-10).

etymology: From the old idea that no two snowflakes are alike, used in the 1990s self-esteem culture ("you are a unique snowflake") and turned on its head by Chuck Palahniuk’s novel Fight Club (1996; film 1999): "You are not a beautiful and unique snowflake." In the 2010s snowflake and "special snowflake" became insults for a person, typically young, thought to be oversensitive, easily offended, and fragile; Claire Fox’s 2016 book helped popularize "Generation Snowflake," and Collins shortlisted "snowflake generation" for its 2016 Word of the Year. It became a common political insult in American culture wars after 2016.
biblical_def: A snowflake, as an insult, is someone who melts at the first sign of heat: easily offended, quick to demand protection from disagreement, convinced of his own uniqueness. The word cuts across two errors at once. The Christian observation: each error is real, and the gospel answers both. The first is the self-esteem gospel that told a generation each child was special in a way that demanded constant affirmation. Scripture affirms that every person is uniquely made by God: "I will praise thee; for I am fearfully and wonderfully made" (Psa 139:14). But that dignity comes from the Maker, not from feelings, and it does not exempt anyone from correction. "Whom the Lord loveth he chasteneth" (Heb 12:6). A generation never told no will struggle to hear the word of God, which says no often. The second error is the fragility itself: the expectation that words that offend must be stopped. Scripture expects believers to be hardy. "Great peace have they which love thy law: and nothing shall offend them" (Psa 119:165). Paul tells Timothy to "endure hardness, as a good soldier of Jesus Christ" (2Ti 2:3). Yet Christians must also beware the insult itself, which is often contempt aimed at the young and the hurting; "Let no corrupt communication proceed out of your mouth" (Eph 4:29). A father tells his children: you are fearfully and wonderfully made, and you are not exempt from hard words; be soft-hearted toward others and hard to offend yourself. And snow is a good picture of something better: "though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow" (Isa 1:18).
webster_summary: Millennial-era insult (Fight Club, 1996; "Generation Snowflake," 2016) for an oversensitive, easily offended person; Scripture grounds uniqueness in the Maker (Psa 139:14), calls believers to be hard to offend (Psa 119:165), and forbids contemptuous speech (Eph 4:29).
webster_full: SNOWFLAKE, n. (Millennial-era slang, 1996–present; insult chiefly from 2016) A person regarded as oversensitive, easily offended, or entitled to special treatment. Also "special snowflake," "snowflake generation."

Webster (1828), root snow: SNOW, noun [Latin nix, nivis; The Latin nivis, is contracted from nigis, like Eng. bow.] 1. Frozen vapor; watery particles congealed into white crystals in the air, and falling to the earth. When there is no wind, these crystals fall in flakes or unbroken collections, sometimes extremely beautiful. 2. A vessel equipped with two masts, resembling the main and fore-masts of a ship, and a third small mast just abaft the mainmast, carrying a try-sail.
Decode for parents: raise children who are tender toward others and tough for themselves; neither fragile nor contemptuous.
scriptures: I will praise thee; for I am fearfully and wonderfully made: marvellous are thy works; and that my soul knoweth right well.
For whom the Lord loveth he chasteneth, and scourgeth every son whom he receiveth.
Great peace have they which love thy law: and nothing shall offend them.
Thou therefore endure hardness, as a good soldier of Jesus Christ.
Come now, and let us reason together, saith the LORD: though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow; though they be red like crimson, they shall be as wool.
corruption_summary: Snowflake names a real fragility bred by self-esteem culture, and is itself often a contemptuous insult; Scripture grounds worth in God, expects hardiness, and forbids corrupt speech.
corruption_paragraphs: Two corruptions meet in the word. The fragility it mocks was bred by a culture that confused love with affirmation and protected children from every disappointment; they arrived at adulthood unprepared for disagreement, criticism, and loss. Scripture’s picture of maturity is the opposite: soldiers who endure hardness, sons who receive chastening. But the insult itself is often cruel, used to dismiss real concerns and to sneer at the young. Contempt is not toughness.

The recovery is the gospel’s order. Worth comes from God and cannot be taken away by insult, so the Christian can afford to be hard to offend. Love comes from God and flows outward, so the Christian can afford to be gentle with the wounded. Teach the young to take correction without melting, to give it without sneering, and to rejoice that the Lord makes scarlet sins white as snow.
roots_summary: Old English snaw (snow) + flake → snowflake → 1990s self-esteem "unique snowflake" → Fight Club (1996) → 2016 "Generation Snowflake" insult.
roots_lines: Old English snaw — snow; Old Norse flaki — a flake
1990s: self-esteem culture, "you are a unique snowflake"
1996: Fight Club, "You are not a beautiful and unique snowflake"
2016: "Generation Snowflake"; Collins shortlist; culture-war insult
Biblical anchor: fearfully and wonderfully made (Psa 139:14); nothing shall offend them (Psa 119:165)
usage: "He called everyone who disagreed with him a snowflake."
Great peace have they which love thy law: and nothing shall offend them (Psa 119:165).
Though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow (Isa 1:18).

etymology: A blend of man and explaining, for a man explaining something to a woman in a condescending way, especially something she already knows better than he does. The word appeared online in 2008, shortly after the writer Rebecca Solnit’s essay "Men Explain Things to Me" (2008), though Solnit did not coin it. The New York Times listed it among words of the year in 2010; online dictionaries added it by 2014. It spawned many blends and became a staple of 2010s gender debate; critics argue it is often used to dismiss any man’s explanation by his sex.
biblical_def: To mansplain is to explain something condescendingly to a woman, assuming she knows less because she is a woman, often when she knows more. The word names a real fault and also carries a framework. The Christian observation: the fault it names is a sin Scripture condemns in anyone. "A fool hath no delight in understanding, but that his heart may discover itself" (Pro 18:2). "He that answereth a matter before he heareth it, it is folly and shame unto him" (Pro 18:13). "Let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak" (Jas 1:19). A man who talks down to his wife, sister, or coworker, assuming ignorance, is proud, and pride is not masculinity. Scripture’s women include Deborah, who judged Israel; Abigail, whose wisdom saved David from bloodshed; and Priscilla, who with her husband "expounded unto him the way of God more perfectly" to the learned Apollos (Act 18:26). Husbands are told to honour their wives "as unto the weaker vessel, and as being heirs together of the grace of life" (1Pe 3:7), weaker in strength, equal in grace. At the same time, the word comes from a framework that interprets relations between the sexes mainly as a contest of power, and it is often used to silence men simply for being men, or to dismiss the biblical teaching of male headship and pastoral office as condescension. A father teaches his son: listen before you speak, never assume a woman knows less, and lead with humility. He teaches his daughter: speak your knowledge with grace, and do not let a slogan teach you that every man who explains something is your enemy.
webster_summary: Millennial-era slang (2008; after Solnit’s essay) for a man’s condescending explanation to a woman; it names real pride Scripture condemns (Pro 18:2; Jas 1:19), within a power-contest framework often used to silence men and dismiss biblical headship.
webster_full: MANSPLAINING, n.; MANSPLAIN, v. (Millennial-era slang, 2008–present; blend of man + explaining) Explaining something to a woman in a condescending manner, often assuming her ignorance. Spawned blends such as -splaining.

Webster (1828), root explain: EXPLAIN, verb transitive [Latin explano; ex and planus, plain, open, smooth.] To make plain, manifest or intelligible; to clear of obscurity; to expound; to illustrate by discourse, or by notes. The first business of a preacher is to explain his text. Notes and comments are intended to explain the scriptures.
Decode for parents: teach sons to listen first and daughters not to read every male explanation as an attack.
scriptures: A fool hath no delight in understanding, but that his heart may discover itself.
He that answereth a matter before he heareth it, it is folly and shame unto him.
Wherefore, my beloved brethren, let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath:
And he began to speak boldly in the synagogue: whom when Aquila and Priscilla had heard, they took him unto them, and expounded unto him the way of God more perfectly.

Likewise, ye husbands, dwell with them according to knowledge, giving honour unto the wife, as unto the weaker vessel, and as being heirs together of the grace of life; that your prayers be not hindered.
corruption_summary: Mansplaining names real male pride that Scripture condemns, but carries a framework that treats the sexes as rivals and is often used to silence men and discredit biblical headship.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is in the framework more than the fault. Condescension is sin, and Christian men should repent of it wherever it appears. But the word was built within a view that sees every interaction between men and women through the lens of power, and in practice it can be used to dismiss any man’s speech by his sex alone, which is itself a kind of prejudice. It is also often aimed at the biblical teaching that men lead in the home and the church, as though headship were merely a habit of talking down.

The recovery is humility in both directions. Biblical headship is servant leadership, modelled on Christ, who washed feet; it has no room for arrogance. Biblical womanhood includes wisdom, teaching of children and younger women, and the courage to speak truth, as Abigail did. Teach the young to listen before speaking, to respect knowledge wherever it is found, and to reject both male arrogance and the slogans that make the sexes enemies.
roots_summary: Man + explain (Latin explanare, to make level, plain) → 2008 mansplaining (after Solnit’s essay) → 2010 NYT words of the year → 2014 dictionaries.
roots_lines: Latin explanare — to flatten, to make plain
2008: Rebecca Solnit, "Men Explain Things to Me"; mansplaining appears online
2010: New York Times words of the year; 2014: online dictionaries
2010s: gender-debate staple; many -splaining blends
Biblical anchor: swift to hear, slow to speak (Jas 1:19); heirs together of the grace of life (1Pe 3:7)
usage: "He explained her own thesis to her. Classic mansplaining."
He that answereth a matter before he heareth it, it is folly (Pro 18:13).
Priscilla and Aquila expounded the way of God to Apollos (Act 18:26).

etymology: From gig, jazz musicians’ slang of the 1920s for a single paid engagement, and economy. The phrase was popularized about 2009, as the financial crisis left many young workers piecing together short-term jobs, and with the rise of app-based platforms: TaskRabbit (2008), Uber (2009), Lyft, DoorDash, Fiverr, Upwork. It describes work organized as independent tasks or contracts rather than steady employment, often without benefits. Millennials, entering the workforce during the Great Recession, became its emblematic workers.
biblical_def: The gig economy is work by the task: driving for an app, delivering food, freelancing projects, a patchwork of short-term jobs instead of a single employer. It offers flexibility and independence, and it often brings insecurity, no benefits, and an endless hustle. Millennials, who came of age in the Great Recession, made it their own. The Christian observation: Scripture says a great deal about work and wages, and much of it applies directly. Work itself is good and commanded: "if any would not work, neither should he eat" (2Th 3:10). Providing for one’s household is a sacred duty: "if any provide not for his own, and specially for those of his own house, he hath denied the faith, and is worse than an infidel" (1Ti 5:8). Scripture also speaks sharply to employers and systems that squeeze workers: "Behold, the hire of the labourers who have reaped down your fields, which is of you kept back by fraud, crieth" (Jas 5:4); "the labourer is worthy of his hire" (Luk 10:7). Day labourers were the gig workers of the Bible, and the law required that they be paid before sundown (Deu 24:15). The gig economy can be an honourable way to earn and provide, and Christians can work in it with diligence and integrity. But it tempts toward two errors: the anxiety that never rests, and the isolation of work without colleagues or community. A father teaches his son to take honest work wherever it is, to work as unto the Lord, to keep the Sabbath even when the app does not, and to aim at building something stable enough to support a family.
webster_summary: Millennial-era term (c. 2009; app platforms) for work by the short-term task or contract; honest labour and provision are commanded (2Th 3:10; 1Ti 5:8), and Scripture also guards the labourer’s wage and rest (Jas 5:4; Deu 24:15).
webster_full: GIG ECONOMY, n. (Millennial-era term, c. 2009–present) An economy of short-term, freelance, or app-based work rather than permanent employment. Related: gig work, side hustle, freelancer.

Webster (1828), root economy: ECONOMY, noun [Latin oeconomia; Gr. house, and law, rule.] 1. Primarily, the management, regulation and government of a family or the concerns of a household. 2. The management of pecuniary concerns or the expenditure of money. Hence, 3. A frugal and judicious use of money; that management which expends money to advantage, and incurs no waste; frugality in the necessary expenditure of money. It differs from parsimony, which implies an improper saving of expense. […]
Decode for parents: honour honest work of every kind, and help your children aim at stability that can support a family.
scriptures: For even when we were with you, this we commanded you, that if any would not work, neither should he eat.
But if any provide not for his own, and specially for those of his own house, he hath denied the faith, and is worse than an infidel.

Behold, the hire of the labourers who have reaped down your fields, which is of you kept back by fraud, crieth: and the cries of them which have reaped are entered into the ears of the Lord of sabaoth.
And in the same house remain, eating and drinking such things as they give: for the labourer is worthy of his hire. Go not from house to house.
At his day thou shalt give him his hire, neither shall the sun go down upon it; for he is poor, and setteth his heart upon it: lest he cry against thee unto the LORD, and it be sin unto thee.
corruption_summary: The gig economy offers flexible honest work, but can breed endless anxiety, isolation, and unprotected labour; Scripture commands work and guards the labourer’s wage and rest.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is twofold. For workers, gig work can become an unending hustle with no rest, no community, and no future, where the app’s demand never stops and Sabbath becomes impossible. For the system, it can shift risk and cost onto the weakest, paying by the task with no regard for the labourer’s life. Scripture condemns both the idle and the exploiter, and it built rest into the week for servants and day labourers alike.

The recovery is work ordered by God. Christians in the gig economy can work with excellence and honesty, keep the Lord’s Day, and use flexibility for family and church rather than for endless earning. Christians who run businesses should pay fairly and promptly, as the law required for the day labourer. Teach the young that every honest job is a calling, and that the goal of work is not the hustle but faithfulness, provision, and generosity.
roots_summary: 1920s jazz gig (a paid engagement) + Greek oikonomia (household management) → economy → c. 2009 gig economy → app platforms of the 2010s.

Greek oikos (house) + nomos (law) → oikonomia → economy
c. 2009: gig economy amid the Great Recession
2008–2015: TaskRabbit, Uber, Lyft, DoorDash, Upwork
Biblical anchor: the labourer is worthy of his hire (Luk 10:7); at his day thou shalt give him his hire (Deu 24:15)
usage: "He drives for two apps and freelances on weekends. Gig economy life."
If any would not work, neither should he eat (2Th 3:10).
The labourer is worthy of his hire (Luk 10:7).

etymology: A self-label for an ambitious young woman running her own business, popular on Instagram from the mid-2010s, in the same family as Sophia Amoruso’s #GIRLBOSS (2014). The hashtag became especially associated with multi-level marketing (MLM) companies, whose recruiters invited women, often young mothers, to become "boss babes" by selling leggings, cosmetics, essential oils, or supplements and recruiting others. By the late 2010s the phrase was widely mocked as MLM jargon, and critics documented that most MLM participants lose money.
biblical_def: A boss babe is a young woman who runs her own business, or says she does: the Instagram entrepreneur with a laptop at the coffee shop, a ring light, and a link in her bio. Often she is selling for a multi-level marketing company and inviting her friends to "join her team." The Christian observation: the virtuous woman of Proverbs is, among other things, a businesswoman. "She considereth a field, and buyeth it: with the fruit of her hands she planteth a vineyard" (Pro 31:16); "She maketh fine linen, and selleth it; and delivereth girdles unto the merchant" (Pro 31:24). Lydia was "a seller of purple" (Act 16:14). Scripture has no objection to women working with skill and earning well, ordered to the good of their households. The examination concerns the culture around the slogan. The "boss babe" image often sells independence from home as the prize and frames success as visible wealth. And the MLM version can be exploitative, turning friendships into sales targets and promising riches most participants never see. "He that maketh haste to be rich shall not be innocent" (Pro 28:20). The virtuous woman’s business served her household; "The heart of her husband doth safely trust in her" (Pro 31:11), and "her children arise up, and call her blessed" (Pro 31:28). A father tells his daughter: use your gifts in business if God leads you there, honestly and diligently; do not sell to your friends what you would not buy yourself; and measure success by faithfulness to your household and your Lord, not by your follower count.
webster_summary: Millennial Instagram self-label (mid-2010s; MLM jargon) for an entrepreneurial young woman; Scripture honours the businesswoman of Proverbs 31 (Pro 31:16, 24), and examines the slogan’s image-selling, its MLM exploitation, and its detachment from household.
webster_full: BOSS BABE, n. (Millennial social-media slang, mid-2010s–present) An ambitious woman running her own business; especially, a recruiter or seller in a multi-level-marketing company. Related: #girlboss, "join my team."
No Webster 1828 entry located for the root boss (an Americanism from Dutch baas).
Decode for parents: encourage your daughter’s gifts for work; warn her about schemes that turn friends into a sales funnel.
scriptures: She considereth a field, and buyeth it: with the fruit of her hands she planteth a vineyard.
She maketh fine linen, and selleth it; and delivereth girdles unto the merchant.
And a certain woman named Lydia, a seller of purple, of the city of Thyatira, which worshipped God, heard us: whose heart the Lord opened, that she attended unto the things which were spoken of Paul.
A faithful man shall abound with blessings: but he that maketh haste to be rich shall not be innocent.
Her children arise up, and call her blessed; her husband also, and he praiseth her.
corruption_summary: Boss babe sells an image of independent wealth and is often MLM recruitment; Scripture honours the enterprising woman whose work serves her household and whose dealings are honest.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is image over substance. The boss-babe aesthetic, laptop, latte, luxury, sells the appearance of success, and in the MLM world the appearance is the product: recruits buy inventory to look like bosses, and most lose money. Friendships become prospect lists. The slogan also frames the household as something to escape and the market as the place of real fulfilment, which reverses the order of Proverbs 31, where enterprise serves the home.

The redemption is honest enterprise ordered to love. The virtuous woman works with her hands, trades wisely, cares for the poor, and is praised in the gates by her works rather than her posts. Teach daughters that business can be a godly calling, that honesty and quality matter more than branding, that friends are not customers, and that the deepest praise a woman can receive is the blessing of her children and the trust of her husband.
